q: What is regularisation and why do deep networks need it?
short: Constraints that stop a model becoming too complex and memorising training data. Deep networks have enough capacity to memorise, so without it they reach perfect training accuracy and poor test accuracy.
detail: Reduces variance at the cost of a little bias.

q: L1 vs L2 regularisation?
short: L2 adds λΣw², shrinks all weights proportionally (weight decay), smooth; L1 adds λΣ|w|, drives some weights exactly to zero (sparsity, feature selection), not differentiable at 0.

q: How does dropout work?
short: During training each unit is dropped with probability p (fresh mask each step); kept units are scaled by 1/(1 − p) (inverted dropout); at inference all units are used.
detail: Prevents co-adaptation; approximates an ensemble of thinned networks.
mistakes: Leaving dropout on at test time.

q: What does batch normalisation do?
short: Normalises each feature to zero mean, unit variance using mini-batch statistics, then applies learnable γ, β; keeps running averages for inference.
detail: Higher learning rates, less init sensitivity, mild regularisation.

q: Batch norm vs layer norm?
short: BN: per feature across the batch, batch-size dependent, running stats, train ≠ test, best for CNNs. LN: per sample across features, batch-independent, same at train and test, best for RNNs/Transformers.

q: Why not initialise all weights to zero?
short: Every neuron in a layer computes the same output and receives the same gradient, so they stay identical: symmetry is never broken.

q: Xavier vs He initialisation?
short: Xavier: Var = 2/(n_in + n_out), for tanh/sigmoid. He: Var = 2/n_in, for ReLU, doubling to compensate for ReLU zeroing half the activations.
mistakes: Using Xavier with deep ReLU nets.

q: What is early stopping?
short: Monitor validation loss; stop when it hasn't improved by min delta for 'patience' epochs; restore the best weights.

q: What is data augmentation? Give examples.
short: Creating label-preserving variations of training data: images (flip, crop, rotate, colour jitter, noise, Cutout, Mixup, CutMix), text (synonym replacement, back-translation).
detail: Only on the training set, after the split.

q: Training accuracy 99%, validation 70%. What do you try?
short: Classic overfitting: add/increase augmentation, dropout, weight decay, early stopping; get more data; reduce capacity; tune on validation.
detail: Check for leakage and distribution differences too.

q: Derive the Xavier variance.
short: Var(z) = n_in Var(w) Var(x) for independent zero-mean terms; forward preservation needs Var(w) = 1/n_in, backward needs 1/n_out; compromise 2/(n_in + n_out). Uniform U(−a, a) has variance a²/3, so a = √(6/(n_in + n_out)).

q: Batch norm on [10, 12, 8, 14] with ε = 0.01, γ = 2, β = 3.
Why does dropout need rescaling, and what is inverted dropout?
short: A unit kept with probability 1 − p has expected output (1 − p)h; to make train and test expectations match, either scale by (1 − p) at test or by 1/(1 − p) during training (inverted, used by frameworks).
follow: Does it match exactly with nonlinearities?

q: Why does L1 produce sparse solutions?
short: Its gradient has constant magnitude λ regardless of |w|, so it keeps pushing small weights to exactly 0 (soft-thresholding); geometrically, loss contours tend to touch the diamond at a corner on an axis.
follow: How to optimise a non-differentiable penalty?
mistakes: Saying L1 is just stronger L2.

q: Your BN model works in training but predictions are poor in deployment with batch size 1.
short: Check model.eval() so running statistics are used; check the running stats were updated on representative data (momentum, enough steps); for genuinely tiny batches during training switch to group/layer norm.
detail: Fine-tuning with frozen BN stats is common.
follow: How do running stats get corrupted?
mistakes: Computing batch stats on a single example.

q: How is regularisation applied differently in CNNs, RNNs and Transformers?
short: CNNs: augmentation, BN, DropBlock/SpatialDropout, global average pooling. RNNs: variational (same-mask) dropout, gradient clipping, layer norm. Transformers: attention/residual dropout, layer norm, label smoothing, warmup, weight decay.
detail: Match the regulariser to the data structure.
mistakes: Fresh dropout masks on recurrent connections.

q: Batch norm and dropout together: what can go wrong?
short: Dropout changes activation variance between training and inference, but BN's running variance was estimated with dropout on: a 'variance shift' at test time. Place dropout after BN (or after the last BN layer) or rely on BN alone.
example: Lower accuracy with dropout before BN.

q: Implement layer norm in NumPy for a (batch, d) array.
short: mu = x.mean(-1, keepdims=True); var = x.var(-1, keepdims=True); y = gamma * (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + eps) + beta.
detail: BN would use axis 0 plus running stats.

q: Show that early stopping approximates L2 regularisation.
short: For a quadratic loss with Hessian eigenvalues λᵢ, GD from 0 for T steps gives component wᵢ = [1 − (1 − ηλᵢ)ᵀ]wᵢ*; L2 with strength α gives λᵢ/(λᵢ + α)·wᵢ*. Matching for small ηλᵢ gives α ≈ 1/(ηT): stopping earlier ≈ stronger penalty.
example: Doubling T halves the effective λ.
follow: What breaks this in deep nets?

q: Derive the bias–variance decomposition.
short: With y = f + ε (E ε = 0, Var σ²): E[(y − f̂)²] = σ² + E[(f − f̂)²]; add and subtract E f̂: (f − E f̂)² + E[(f̂ − E f̂)²]; cross terms vanish. Bias² + variance + noise.

q: Why does batch norm help optimisation? Is it really covariate shift?
short: Original motivation: reduce internal covariate shift. Later evidence (Santurkar et al.) suggests the main effect is a smoother loss landscape (better-conditioned gradients), enabling larger learning rates; BN also makes layers scale-invariant to their weights, and its batch noise regularises.
detail: With BN, weight decay mainly raises the effective learning rate.
follow: What replaces BN in normalisation-free nets?
mistakes: Stating covariate shift as settled fact.

q: Design a regularisation plan for a 50-layer CNN on 20k medical images.
short: He init, Conv → BN → ReLU with residual connections; pretrained backbone (transfer); domain-valid augmentation (flips/rotations/intensity, not unrealistic ones); weight decay 1e-4; dropout before the classifier; label smoothing; early stopping on a patient-level validation split; monitor train–val gap and calibration.
detail: Split by patient to avoid leakage.
mistakes: Image-level split with multiple images per patient.

q: Explain DropBlock and variational dropout: why structured dropout?
short: When activations are correlated (neighbouring pixels, consecutive time steps), dropping independent elements removes little information. DropBlock drops contiguous spatial blocks; variational dropout reuses one mask across time so the recurrent noise doesn't compound and memory isn't destroyed.
mistakes: Using plain dropout on conv feature maps and expecting much effect.

q: How do Mixup and label smoothing regularise?
short: Both soften targets: Mixup trains on convex combinations of inputs and labels, encouraging linear behaviour between examples and smaller margins of overconfidence; label smoothing caps the target probability at 1 − ε, preventing logits from growing without bound. Both improve calibration and robustness.
follow: Why can label smoothing hurt distillation?
mistakes: Using Mixup labels as hard labels.
